intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-89 (DEE89) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the GAD1 gene (605363) on chromosome 2q31.1.

paragraphs.text: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-89 (DEE89) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic GAD1 mutations. Seizures begin in the neonatal period or early infancy, and affected individuals have hypotonia and severe developmental delay. Non-central nervous system features vary and include skeletal abnormalities, dysmorphic features and cleft palate (Neuray et al., 2020). Chatron et al. (2020) also reported joint contractures, pes equinovarus and omphalocele.

paragraphs.text: Chatron et al. (2020) reported 11 patients from 6 unrelated consanguineous families of Algerian, Egyptian, Turkish, Iranian and Brazilian origin with a syndromic developmental and epileptic encephalopathy. In all patients, seizures began in the first 2 months of life, mainly as epileptic spasms or myoclonic seizures. Early EEG showed suppression-burst, burst attenuation or hypsarrhythmia. Eight patients had joint contractures and/or pes equinovarus, 7 had cleft palate and 2 had omphalocele. All living patients had profound psychomotor delay, and 4 died before 4 years of age.

paragraphs.text: In Family A, Chatron et al. (2020) described 2 sibs, a boy and a girl, born to Algerian first-cousin parents. Both had cleft soft palate. By 5 months of age the boy had developmental regression, axial hypotonia and hypsarrhythmia. At 6 years he had spastic tetraparesis and no speech. His sister had spasms from 2 days of age, and her EEG showed suppression-burst. Levetiracetam and vigabatrin controlled her seizures by 3 months, but she had severe developmental delay with axial hypotonia.

paragraphs.text: Neuray et al. (2020) reported 6 patients (3 male and 3 female) from 6 unrelated families of Persian, Pakistani, African American, Sudanese, Egyptian and Turkish ancestry. Four of the families were consanguineous. Seizures began between 2 and 6 months of age and were mainly focal motor seizures. Some patients also had epileptic spasms, focal non-motor seizures or bilateral motor seizures. Medication controlled seizures in 3 patients, and 3 were drug-resistant. At seizure onset, EEG showed burst suppression in 2 patients, diffuse slowing with multifocal and generalized sharp waves in 2, and hypsarrhythmia in 2. Brain MRI was normal except in 2 patients: 1 had slight ventricular enlargement and 1 had moderate global atrophy. All patients had severe developmental delay, and most never developed speech or nonverbal communication. Intellectual disability was severe in 5 patients and moderate in 1. Five patients had reduced muscle strength or tone. Of these, 4 lacked head control or could not sit or crawl, and 2 depended on a nasogastric tube because of dysphagia. Four patients had mild facial dysmorphism, and 1 had cleft palate. Other features with no common pattern included hirsutism, kidney stones, urogenital malformations, diastasis recti, reduced head circumference, clinodactyly, short arms, arthrogryposis of the lower limbs, congenital hip dislocation, high myopia and hearing impairment. Metabolic workups were normal. Cognitive development did not improve even when seizures were controlled: 3 of the 6 patients became seizure-free, yet all had severe intellectual disability. The authors hypothesized that GAD1 variants affect development independently of seizure control.

paragraphs.text: In a Persian girl with DEE89 born to double-first-cousin parents (Family A), Neuray et al. (2020) used exome sequencing to identify a homozygous c.1691A-G transition in the GAD1 gene, resulting in an asn564-to-ser (N564S) substitution. Her phenotype was relatively mild: she had moderate intellectual disability, simple speech, and seizures that became controlled. The variant had been seen once in the heterozygous state in gnomAD and had a CADD score of 26.1. SIFT, MutationTaster and PolyPhen-2 predicted it to be pathogenic. It lies in the C-terminal catalytic domain, and in silico analysis predicted reduced protein stability.

paragraphs.text: In a Sudanese boy with DEE89 whose parents were second cousins (Family D), Neuray et al. (2020) identified a homozygous c.1040C-T transition in the GAD1 gene, resulting in a thr347-to-met (T347M) substitution. He had epileptic spasms with hypsarrhythmia, severe hypotonia and severe dysmorphic features. The variant had been reported twice in the heterozygous state in gnomAD and had a CADD score of 29.1. In silico analysis predicted that it breaks hydrogen bonds in the PLP-binding domain. A heterozygous sister had a different neurodevelopmental condition without seizures.
